Dx​x=12​⟨τ^x​x(0)+τ^x​x(1)⟩−(Dpara00+Dpara01+Dpara11),D_{xx}=\frac{1}{2}\big\langle\hat{\tau}^{(0)}_{xx}+\hat{\tau}^{(1)}_{xx}\big\rangle-\big(D^{00}_{\text{para}}+D^{01}_{\text{para}}+D^{11}_{\text{para}}\big), (31)

we find that the phonon-assisted contribution is nearly self-canceling: across the considered temperatures, 12​⟨τ^x​x(1)⟩−Dpara01−Dpara11\frac{1}{2}\langle\hat{\tau}^{(1)}_{xx}\rangle-D^{01}_{\text{para}}-D^{11}_{\text{para}} remains a small fraction of the total diamagnetic weight, so the phonon-assisted current generates substantial finite-frequency spectral weight while consuming almost exactly its own contribution to the optical sum rule. This leaves Dx​xD_{xx} governed by the competition between the electronic stress ⟨τ^x​x(0)⟩\langle\hat{\tau}^{(0)}_{xx}\rangle and the electronic relaxation term Dpara00D^{00}_{\text{para}}; in the Holstein model, the Drude weight is governed entirely by this competition. The two models differ sharply in how the electronic paramagnetic term exhausts its sum-rule reservoir (see Fig. 9(d)): the Holstein ratio Dpara00/(⟨τ^x​x(0)⟩/2)D_{\text{para}}^{00}/(\langle\hat{\tau}^{(0)}_{xx}\rangle/2) grows rapidly with temperature, effectively extinguishing the Drude weight by T=0.4T=0.4, whereas the corresponding BSSH ratio begins at a higher magnitude but saturates more slowly. Consistently, the contributions to the Drude weight from each momentum sector (D𝐊D_{\mathbf{K}}, Eq. 30 restricted to one 𝐊\mathbf{K} sector) show no analog of the Holstein collapse: the ratio D𝐊/(⟨τ^⟩𝐊/2)D_{\mathbf{K}}/(\langle\hat{\tau}\rangle_{\mathbf{K}}/2) for the band-edge states that dominate the thermal ensemble remains comparable to its Γ\Gamma-point value, so thermal population replaces the ground state with states of similar ballistic character, reordering the Holstein and BSSH Drude weights at moderate temperature despite the stronger BSSH dressing at the same coupling.

V.4 Towards ab initio simulations

To demonstrate that our current framework can be applied with ab initio electron–phonon matrix elements without additional model assumptions, we evaluate the lithium fluoride (LiF) electron- and hole-polaron binding energies using the momentum-space Hamiltonian in Eq. 1. LiF has become a standard benchmark for ab initio polaron methods, having been studied extensively with the Green’s function (GF) and ab initio polaron-equation approaches of Giustino and co-workers [122, 121, 72, 26], the canonical-transformation and first-principles DiagMC approaches of Bernardi and co-workers [76, 83], and recent variational and NNQS wavefunction methods [84, 5, 114]. For a sequence of uniform 𝐤\mathbf{k}-meshes ranging from size 333^{3} to 21321^{3} for the electron polaron and 333^{3} to 15315^{3} for the hole, we optimize the first-order dCC wavefunction and report the binding energy relative to the free-electron limit, Ebind=Efree−EpolE_{\text{bind}}=E_{\text{free}}-E_{\text{pol}}, in Fig. 10.

Even at the system sizes considered, a linear extrapolation [86] of the binding energies obtained from the densest three meshes yields excellent agreement with recent state-of-the-art values, as summarized in Table 3 [5, 84, 114, 83]. In particular, dCC-1-S1 yields a higher binding energy and, therefore, a lower variational total energy than recent NNQS results across all considered grid sizes, and largely closes the energy gap between dD2 and DiagMC. This indicates that our present ansatz may be more expressive or easier to optimize than NNQS at practically accessible network depths. Our extrapolated LiF electron-polaron binding energies agree closely with published DiagMC [83] and dD2 [5] results obtained from large grids. As the dCC extrapolation uses mesh sizes no larger than 21321^{3}, some residual finite-size error is expected; a comparison between dD2 extrapolations on the same meshes and dD2’s thermodynamic limit (TDL) suggests that our extrapolated value remains slightly underbound relative to the true dCC TDL estimate.

For the hole polaron, our result is consistent with GF, NNQS, variational, and perturbative approaches, but remains substantially below the reported DiagMC binding energy. We note that the hole polaron lies deep in the strong-coupling regime, where the diagrammatic expansion converges most slowly and residual bias is most difficult to remove [5]. Variational ansätze of very different form, the coherent-state-based dD2 and dCC wavefunctions and the NNQS parameterization, agree to within roughly 0.020.02 eV of one another. The published dD2 value was obtained on meshes larger than ours, making residual finite-size error an unlikely explanation for the gap. Attributing the discrepancy entirely to missing correlation would require these very different wavefunction forms to miss nearly identical amounts of correlation energy, suggesting that part of it may instead reflect bias in the diagrammatic reference.

The first-order dCC ansatz is structurally close to coherent-state second-order perturbation theory (CSPT2) [75, 114]: both introduce one-phonon excitations above a displaced phonon vacuum, but CSPT2 determines the amplitudes perturbatively on an unprojected reference and evaluates the energy through second order, whereas dCC determines them variationally on a momentum-projected one. The variational optimization retains the coherent-state description where it is adequate (strong coupling) while capturing one-phonon corrections that CSPT2 represents only perturbatively.

VI Conclusions and Outlook

We have introduced dCC, a translationally invariant variational coupled-cluster theory for single polarons. Three structural features make this nonperturbative framework practical: momentum projection restores the translational symmetry broken by the coherent-state reference and gives direct access to polaron energy bands; the single-carrier structure admits closed-form variational energies at cost as low as 𝒪⁡(N3)\mathcal{O}(N^{3}); and the coherent-state reference requires no explicit phonon-number cutoff. The same excitation hierarchy that systematically improves the ground state extends, through the projected tangent-space response formalism, to spectral functions and optical conductivities at zero and finite temperature, with thermal phonon traces evaluated analytically rather than by enumerating thermally occupied phonon-number configurations. The theory thus bridges longstanding coupled-cluster ideas from electronic structure and variational ansätze developed for modern polaron problems.

We validated the framework across the canonical polaron models. dCC ground-state energies closely track DMRG, NNQS, and DiagMC benchmarks for the one- and two-dimensional Holstein and SSH (optical and bond) models, reproduce Lanczos polaron band structures even for dispersive phonons, and lie closer to DiagMC than Feynman’s variational solution for the Fröhlich model at most couplings considered. The tangent-space response reproduces Lanczos and TD-DMRG spectral functions and optical conductivities in one dimension at zero and finite temperature, and extends momentum-resolved finite-temperature spectra to two-dimensional lattices beyond the practical reach of these methods. Applied directly to ab initio electron–phonon matrix elements, dCC yields LiF electron- and hole-polaron binding energies in agreement with state-of-the-art many-body methods, with a lower variational energy than NNQS.

Owing to its low-order polynomial scaling, the ground-state framework applies to materials-specific Hamiltonians without modification, and its integration with recently developed electron–phonon compression schemes [82] should enable material properties to be converged to the TDL. The variational structure also invites extensions to bipolarons, where two carriers interact with a shared phonon environment, and to time-dependent variational principle algorithms for excited-state and non-equilibrium dynamics across wider parameter regimes and temperatures.

More broadly, this work demonstrates that quantum-chemical many-body methods and traditional polaron approaches have much to offer each other. The coupled-cluster formalism developed here provides a unified variational treatment of electron–phonon polaron ground states and dynamics, and we hope that related ideas may be brought to bear on other polaronic problems of modern interest, including Bose and spin polarons.

Appendices

Appendix A Computational Details

DMRG reference values are obtained with the Renormalizer package [112]. Finite-temperature DMRG spectra are obtained with thermofield dynamics using a bond dimension of 700700 with a phonon cutoff of 3232 per mode for T≥0.4T\geq 0.4 and bond dimension 128128 with per-mode phonon cutoff 1212 for lower temperatures so that lineshapes are qualitatively converged. We use a time step of Δ​t=0.1\Delta t=0.1 with a total time of tmax=150t_{\text{max}}=150 (tmax=80t_{\text{max}}=80 for T=0.2T=0.2). The dCC variational parameters were optimized by direct minimization of the energy using analytic gradients and diagonal Hessian preconditioning. Optimizations were performed in Python using either geometric direct-minimization (GDM) [128] implemented in a development version of Q–Chem [33], or a line-search limited memory BFGS (L-BFGS-LS) implementation in JAX [13, 8]. For the ab initio calculations, we work directly with the ab initio band-dispersion ϵi𝐤\epsilon_{i_{\mathbf{k}}}, phonon frequencies ων​𝐪\omega_{\nu\mathbf{q}}, and electron–phonon couplings gi​jν​(𝐤,𝐪)g^{\nu}_{ij}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q}) generated from Quantum Espresso [43] and EPW [106], retaining all six phonon branches and relevant electronic bands.

Appendix D Fröhlich model

In this appendix, we detail the discretization procedure, reference states employed, and the continuum-extrapolation protocol underlying the Fröhlich results reported in Section V.1.3. The imposition of a periodic finite system volume Ω\Omega in the Fröhlich coupling gF​(𝐪)g_{\text{F}}(\mathbf{q}) restricts the allowed momenta to the set 2​πL​ℤ3\frac{2\pi}{L}\mathbb{Z}^{3}, where Ω=L3\Omega=L^{3}.

The discretization of the real-space volume element with a grid of spacing a=LNa=\frac{L}{N} further restricts the set of allowed momenta to

𝐤=2​πL​𝐧,ni∈{−N2,…,N2−1}\mathbf{k}=\frac{2\pi}{L}\mathbf{n},\quad n_{i}\in\left\{-\frac{N}{2},\dots,\frac{N}{2}-1\right\} (A26)

so that each Cartesian component is bounded by the momentum cutoff kmax=πak_{\text{max}}=\frac{\pi}{a}. Momentum addition 𝐤+𝐪\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q} is folded back onto the grid modulo 2​πa\frac{2\pi}{a}. The discretized model thus has two parameters with disjoint physical roles: the box size L=N​aL=Na controls the infrared behavior, while the cutoff kmax=πak_{\text{max}}=\frac{\pi}{a} controls the ultraviolet. The continuum Fröhlich model is then recovered in the ordered double limit L→∞L\rightarrow\infty at fixed aa, followed by a→0a\rightarrow 0. Such a procedure is necessary as the limit a→0a\rightarrow 0 at fixed NN results in an increasingly small volume and does not converge.

The Fröhlich coupling g𝐪g_{\mathbf{q}} at 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 is formally singular and requires careful handling on a discrete grid. Though this element is conventionally excluded, that exclusion leads to a slowly converging finite-size error. As the 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 phonon mode couples exactly to the total electron number ∑𝐤a𝐤†​a𝐤\sum_{\mathbf{k}}a^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{k}}a_{\mathbf{k}}, which is unity for the single electron considered here, its Hamiltonian contribution is that of a displaced harmonic oscillator, which decouples exactly and contributes −g𝟎2-g_{\mathbf{0}}^{2} to the ground-state energy for any value assigned to the coupling g𝟎g_{\mathbf{0}} at that point. On a finite grid, the singular grid point represents a momentum space cell of volume Ω0=(2​π)3Ω\Omega_{0}=\frac{(2\pi)^{3}}{\Omega}. Though the Fröhlich coupling element is singular at this point, its corresponding contribution to the energy is finite at finite LL because the 1q2\frac{1}{q^{2}} singularity in |g𝐪|2|g_{\mathbf{q}}|^{2} is integrable in three dimensions due to its cancellation with the three-dimensional volume element. Viewing the discrete grid as a midpoint quadrature approximation of the continuum limit, we therefore replace the singular 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 contribution with an effective central cell coupling chosen to approximate the integrated value of |g𝐪|2|g_{\mathbf{q}}|^{2} over that cell, analogous to standard treatments of integrable long-wavelength singularities in periodic calculations [19, 38]. We approximate the integration volume with an equivalent volume sphere with radius qc=(3​Ω04​π)1/3q_{c}=\left(\frac{3\Omega_{0}}{4\pi}\right)^{1/3}, and obtain the analytic average in the central cell of

⟨g𝐪2⟩0\displaystyle\langle g_{\mathbf{q}}^{2}\rangle_{0} =1Ω0​∫0qc∫0π∫02​π23/2​π​αΩ​1q2​q2​sin⁡(θ)​𝑑q​𝑑θ​𝑑ϕ\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\Omega_{0}}\int_{0}^{q_{c}}\int_{0}^{\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\frac{2^{3/2}\pi\alpha}{\Omega}\frac{1}{q^{2}}q^{2}\sin(\theta)dqd\theta d\phi (A27)
=2​απ​qc\displaystyle=\frac{\sqrt{2}\alpha}{\pi}q_{c}
=2​α​(6π)1/3​1L.\displaystyle={\sqrt{2}\alpha}\left(\frac{6}{\pi}\right)^{1/3}\frac{1}{L}.

We thus see that excluding the 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 element introduces a finite-size error which decays as O⁡(L−1)O(L^{-1}), and replace the singular coupling with ⟨g𝐪2⟩0\sqrt{\langle g_{\mathbf{q}}^{2}\rangle_{0}} analogous to procedures employed in previous studies [129, 96]. As this mode couples only to the total electron number and thus decouples completely, the error incurred by approximating the volume with a spherical cell vanishes identically in the reported corrected values, in which this error cancels with the subtracted auxiliary quantity sharing this approximation.

D.1 Reference choice

The dCC calculations of this appendix employ the discrete machinery of the main text and require only a suitable choice of reference state. We use a coherent-state product reference in which the electron occupies an orbital drawn from a one-parameter family, with coherent-state shifts determined self-consistently from the electronic density. For α≤9\alpha\leq 9, we use a Gaussian orbital of width σ\sigma, while for α≥10\alpha\geq 10 we use the scaled Pekar orbital

φw​(𝐫)=(α​w)3/2​φP​(α​w​𝐫)\varphi_{w}(\mathbf{r})=(\alpha w)^{3/2}\varphi_{\text{P}}(\alpha w\mathbf{r}) (A28)

where φP​(𝐫)\varphi_{\text{P}}(\mathbf{r}) minimizes the strong-coupling Pekar functional [105, 59] at unit coupling and is obtained numerically. As the Pekar orbital is only exact in the adiabatic continuum limit, the scaling parameter ww is retained to absorb the leading finite-grid and finite-α\alpha corrections to the orbital profile. In particular, the scale parameter (σ\sigma or ww) is chosen to minimize the closed-form discrete grid energy with the constraint that the kinetic energy of the discrete orbital match its continuum counterpart to a fixed tolerance. This guards against artificial overbinding of the polaron for sufficiently localized states caused by the saturation of kinetic energy at the fixed momentum cutoff scale and the continual growth of the Fröhlich binding energy. Importantly, the continuum reference energy remains analytic as a homogeneous function of the scaling parameter ww, which allows the exact finite-size and finite-cutoff error of the discrete reference to be determined in closed form. As an additional safeguard, the momentum-space grid weight of the optimized dCC electronic field is verified to vanish at the grid edge, which excludes the artificially overbound lattice states, whose weight there remains O⁡(1)O(1).

D.2 Finite-size correction and continuum convergence

Each converged dCC energy is corrected by the exact discretization error of an auxiliary energy, whose continuum limit is known in closed form. We apply three such auxiliary quantities.

With reference orbital coefficients ϕ𝐤\phi_{\mathbf{k}} and the grid-density form

n𝐪=∑𝐤ϕ𝐤+𝐪∗​ϕ𝐤,n_{\mathbf{q}}=\sum_{\mathbf{k}}\phi^{*}_{\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q}}\phi_{\mathbf{k}}, (A29)

the minimized product state reference energy on the grid takes the closed form

Erefgrid=∑𝐤|𝐤|22​|ϕ𝐤|2−∑𝐪g𝐪2​n𝐪2,E^{\text{grid}}_{\text{ref}}=\sum_{\mathbf{k}}\frac{|\mathbf{k}|^{2}}{2}|\phi_{\mathbf{k}}|^{2}-\sum_{\mathbf{q}}g_{\mathbf{q}}^{2}n_{\mathbf{q}}^{2}, (A30)

while its continuum limit remains analytic for every reference we employ. We then have E∞​(σ)=34​σ2−ασ​πE^{\infty}(\sigma)=\frac{3}{4\sigma^{2}}-\frac{\alpha}{\sigma\sqrt{\pi}} for the Gaussian family, and E∞​(α,w)=α2​(T1​w2−C1​w)E^{\infty}(\alpha,w)=\alpha^{2}(T_{1}w^{2}-C_{1}w) for the scaled Pekar orbital, where

T1=12​∫|∇φP|2=0.108513,and ​C1=2​T1T_{1}=\frac{1}{2}\int|\nabla\varphi_{\text{P}}|^{2}=0.108513,\quad\text{and }C_{1}=2T_{1} (A31)

by the virial condition. The third auxiliary is second-order perturbation theory, which is not used as a reference, but has grid value EgridPT2=−∑𝐪g𝐪21+|𝐪|2/2E^{\text{grid}}_{\text{PT2}}=-\sum_{\mathbf{q}}\frac{g_{\mathbf{q}}^{2}}{1+|\mathbf{q}|^{2}/2} and continuum limit EPT2∞=−αE^{\infty}_{\text{PT2}}=-\alpha. As the dCC ansatz is complete in the one-phonon excitation sector, its optimized amplitudes at weak coupling assume the exact perturbative values at every retained momentum, and the discretization error of the dCC energy thus coincides with that of second-order perturbation theory to leading order in the coupling.

We then report

Ecorrected=EdCC+[Eaux∞−Eauxgrid]E_{\text{corrected}}=E_{\text{dCC}}+\left[E^{\infty}_{\text{aux}}-E^{\text{grid}}_{\text{aux}}\right] (A32)

where the bracketed expression is the exact finite-size and finite-cutoff correction of the auxiliary and independent of the dCC optimization and benchmark quantities, so that Eq. A32 removes from the dCC energy the part of its discretization error which the auxiliary shares. Writing δ​X=Xgrid−X∞\delta X=X^{\text{grid}}-X^{\infty}, we have

Ecorrected−EdCC∞=δ⁡(EdCC−Eaux)E_{\text{corrected}}-E^{\infty}_{\text{dCC}}=\delta(E_{\text{dCC}}-E_{\text{aux}}) (A33)

which is small precisely when the auxiliary quantity shares the same physical structure as our ansatz, which is perturbative at weak couplings and adiabatic at strong couplings. The auxiliary is selected by two a priori rules. First, the auxiliary must carry a discretization error of definite sign, as the dCC error it corrects approaches from one side. The perturbative auxiliary loses this property for α≳8\alpha\gtrsim 8, where its infrared and ultraviolet errors enter with opposing signs and become comparable within our range of box sizes, so that the bracket passes through zero mid sequence with respect to the grid size. Second, among the qualified auxiliaries, we select the one whose corrected sequence is flattest across the largest grids employed, with agreement between independent auxiliaries serving as a consistency check. The corrected energy is thus a finite-size corrected estimate with a controlled residual and is not guaranteed to be variational, while the raw energy of each grid remains a strict upper bound of the discretized model. The auxiliary dependence itself diminishes systematically with cutoff, with the perturbative and Gaussian corrections at α=6\alpha=6 approaching one another from opposite sides as kmaxk_{\text{max}} grows, so that the selection matters least where the extrapolation is read.

The two continuum limits are treated in separate ways suitable for their measured residuals. The box limit is read directly at its demonstrated plateau over the largest grids, where the final box size changes the energy by less than 6×10−36\times 10^{-3} per unit coupling, and is not extrapolated. The momentum cutoff is extrapolated with a power law form, and the box-converged plateaus drawn from kmax/α={1.4,1.75,2,2.5,3}k_{\text{max}}/\alpha=\{1.4,1.75,2,2.5,3\}, subject to the infrared floor kmax≥4k_{\text{max}}\geq 4 are extrapolated as

E⁡(kmax)=E∞+c​kmax−pE(k_{\text{max}})=E_{\infty}+ck_{\text{max}}^{-p} (A34)

with a single exponent shared across all couplings and per-α\alpha coefficients E∞,cE_{\infty},c. An exponent fit per α\alpha would render each three-point fit exactly determined, while the shared exponent leaves one validating degree of freedom per coupling and yields p≃2.5p\simeq 2.5. Reported uncertainties vary the exponent over p∈[1.6,3.6]p\in[1.6,3.6], which is determined by considering the range of pp which produce a residual within two times that of the optimized pp. The power law form is validated at α=10\alpha=10, where a fourth cutoff kmax=3​αk_{\text{max}}=3\alpha was computed after fitting and agrees with the fit-prediction to 3×10−43\times 10^{-4} per unit coupling. We use the same data to isolate the pure cutoff error by comparing simulations done with identical box sizes.

The D2 (Landau–Pekar) product ansatz energy was separately computed directly on discretized grids at a fixed ultraviolet cutoff of kmax/α=4k_{\text{max}}/\alpha=4 which was numerically confirmed to leave a negligible residual contribution to the ground-state energy. The resulting energies obtained on different box sizes were then extrapolated with respect to the box length LL. As the D2 ansatz reduces to the Pekar functional in the continuum limit, which has a known global minimum of E∞/α2=−0.108513E_{\infty}/\alpha^{2}=-0.108513 [105, 59], this provides a check against a known limit.

D.3 Ground-state energies and benchmark comparison

Table A1 collects the dCC ground-state energies across the coupling range together with digitized diagrammatic Monte Carlo values [51]. A comparison of the ground-state energies obtained via different methods is shown in Fig. 3. The raw energy of the largest grid run at a reference cutoff kmax=2​αk_{\text{max}}=2\alpha is reported unmodified, and serves as a variational upper bound to the corresponding discretized model. The continuum estimate E∞E_{\infty} follows the protocol of Appendix D.2, and its quoted uncertainty represents half the spread in energy obtained by refitting each coupling with the exponent range endpoints {1.6,3.6}\{1.6,3.6\}. Only α=1\alpha=1 is reported with no extrapolation. At α=1\alpha=1, all cutoff ratios fall below the floor kmax=4k_{\text{max}}=4, and we thus report the converged value at kmax=4k_{\text{max}}=4 directly.

At weak couplings, the corrected energies are in excellent quantitative agreement with the benchmark where the perturbative matching of the one-phonon sector operates. The deviation achieves its maximum in the crossover regime of approximately 2.54%2.54\% at α=8\alpha=8 where neither the perturbative nor adiabatic description is sufficiently accurate. This error progressively decreases at stronger couplings where the scaled Pekar reference becomes increasingly accurate. Though each extrapolated energy lies above the benchmark, the lower edge of the exponent band extends between 0.1%0.1\% and 1.4%1.4\% below the digitized values across α=11−15\alpha=11-15, with the extrapolated limit and rest of the band lying above.

Appendix E Additional numerical results

E.1 Dispersive-phonon band structure

We augment the 1D Holstein model with a phonon hopping tph​∑ibi+1†​bi+h.c.t_{\text{ph}}\sum_{i}b^{\dagger}_{i+1}b_{i}+\text{h.c.}, which yields the phonon dispersion ω⁡(q)=ω0+2​tph​cos⁡(q)\omega(q)=\omega_{0}+2t_{\text{ph}}\cos(q) with ω0\omega_{0} the Einstein frequency.

Figure A1 compares the resulting polaron band structure with numerically exact Lanczos benchmarks obtained directly in the thermodynamic limit [11] and NNQS calculations on a 42-site lattice [84]. dD2 is highly accurate at small polaron momenta for this coupling type but incurs a large error near the Brillouin-zone edge, which the first-order correlated excitations in dCC-1-S1 correct.

E.2 Real-space observables

For the Holstein model, the density-displacement correlation

CH​(𝐫):=⟨∑in^i​X^i+𝐫⟩,C_{\text{H}}(\mathbf{r}):=\langle\sum_{i}\hat{n}_{i}\hat{X}_{i+\mathbf{r}}\rangle, (A35)

with X^i\hat{X}_{i} the displacement operator bi†+bib^{\dagger}_{i}+b_{i}, measures the lattice deformation around the carrier, while for the BSSH model the corresponding bond correlation function in the xx-direction,

CBx​(𝐫):=⟨∑i(ai+x^†​ai+ai†​ai+x^)​X^i+𝐫x⟩,C_{\text{B}}^{x}(\mathbf{r}):=\langle\sum_{i}(a^{\dagger}_{i+\hat{x}}a_{i}+a^{\dagger}_{i}a_{i+\hat{x}})\hat{X}^{x}_{i+\mathbf{r}}\rangle, (A36)

characterizes the degree to which the electron–phonon interaction modulates the hopping along a given direction. We additionally compute the quasiparticle weight Zk=|⟨0|​ak​|Ψ⟩|2/⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩Z_{k}=|\bra{0}a_{k}\ket{\Psi}|^{2}/\innerproduct{\Psi}{\Psi} for the ground state |Ψ⟩\ket{\Psi} and the average phonon number Nph=⟨∑ibi†​bi⟩N_{\text{ph}}=\langle\sum_{i}b^{\dagger}_{i}b_{i}\rangle as functions of coupling strength in the anti-adiabatic regime ω≫t\omega\gg t. The results are shown in Fig. A2 and discussed in the main text.

Appendix F Tangent-space structure

In the following, we will detail the tangent-space basis states included within the first- and second-order levels of excited state theory, working in a real-space, single-band formalism suitable for the model systems considered for simplicity. Throughout this appendix, both the reference wavefunction and its tangent vectors use unnormalized Bargmann coherent states for simplicity. In this setting, the first-order wavefunction may be expressed as

|ΨdCC-1-S1⟩\displaystyle\ket{\Psi_{\text{dCC-1-S1}}} =Ξ^​eT^​|ΨD​2⟩\displaystyle=\hat{\Xi}e^{\hat{T}}\ket{\Psi_{\text{D}2}} (A37)
=Ξ^​eT^​(∑lψl​al†​|0⟩el⊗exp⁡(∑mαm​bm†)​|0⟩ph)\displaystyle=\hat{\Xi}e^{\hat{T}}\left(\sum_{l}\psi_{l}a^{\dagger}_{l}\ket{0}_{\text{el}}\otimes\exp(\sum_m \alpha_m b^\dagger_m)\ket{0}_{\text{ph}}\right)
=Ξ^​(∑lζl​al†​|0⟩el⊗|𝚯⟩+∑l​mγl,m​al†​|0⟩el⊗bm†​|𝚯⟩)\displaystyle=\hat{\Xi}\left(\sum_{l}\zeta_{l}a^{\dagger}_{l}\ket{0}_{\text{el}}\otimes\ket{\boldsymbol\Theta}+\sum_{lm}\gamma_{l,m}a^{\dagger}_{l}\ket{0}_{\text{el}}\otimes b^{\dagger}_{m}\ket{\boldsymbol\Theta}\right)

where the coherent state shifts 𝚯:=𝜶+𝜷\bm{\Theta}:=\bm{\alpha}+\bm{\beta} are composed of a fixed part 𝜶\bm{\alpha} obtained from the reference D2 calculation and a component 𝜷:=(t1,t2,⋯,tN)\bm{\beta}:=(t_{1},t_{2},\cdots,t_{N}) introduced through the coupled cluster operator eT^ph=exp⁡(∑ltl​bl†)e^{\hat{T}_{\text{ph}}}=\exp(\sum_l t_l b^\dagger_l) . We have additionally defined the single-band specializations of ζl\zeta_{l} and γl,m\gamma_{l,m} defined in terms of the real-space coupled-cluster amplitudes and D2 electronic parameters ({ψ}\{\psi\})

ζl:=ψl+∑at0a​ψl,a\zeta_{l}:=\psi_{l}+\sum_{a}t_{0}^{a}\psi_{l,a} (A38)
γl,m:=∑at0,ma​ψl,a\gamma_{l,m}:=\sum_{a}t_{0,m}^{a}\psi_{l,a} (A39)

where 00 denotes the single occupied electronic orbital and aa labeling the virtual orbitals (ψ1,a,…​ψN,a\psi_{1,a},...\psi_{N,a}) defined to form a complete orthonormal set.

As discussed in the main text, the tangent states are obtained by taking derivatives of the ground-state wavefunction with respect to the variational parameters. At the first-order level of theory for the ground state, there are three types of parameters describing electronic, phonon, and coupled electron–phonon degrees of freedom. This leads to the three types of tangent states

|1e⟩\displaystyle\ket{1_\text{e}} :=∂∂t0a​|ΨdCC-1-S1⟩=Ξ^​(∑l→ψl→,a​al†​|0⟩el⊗|𝚯⟩)\displaystyle:=\frac{\partial}{\partial t_{0}^{a}}\ket{\Psi_{\text{dCC-1-S1}}}=\hat{\Xi}\left(\sum_{\vec{l}}\psi_{\vec{l},a}a^{\dagger}_{l}\ket{0}_{\text{el}}\otimes\ket{\boldsymbol\Theta}\right) (A40)
|2p⟩\displaystyle\ket{2_\text{p}} :=∂∂tz​|ΨdCC-1-S1⟩=Ξ^​(∑l→ζl→​al→†​|0⟩el⊗bz→†​|𝚯⟩+∑l→​k→γl→,k→​al→†​|0⟩el⊗bk→†​bz→†​|𝚯⟩)\displaystyle:=\frac{\partial}{\partial t_{z}}\ket{\Psi_{\text{dCC-1-S1}}}=\hat{\Xi}\left(\sum_{\vec{l}}\zeta_{\vec{l}}a^{\dagger}_{\vec{l}}\ket{0}_{\text{el}}\otimes b^{\dagger}_{\vec{z}}\ket{\boldsymbol\Theta}+\sum_{\vec{l}\vec{k}}\gamma_{\vec{l},\vec{k}}a^{\dagger}_{\vec{l}}\ket{0}_{\text{el}}\otimes b^{\dagger}_{\vec{k}}b^{\dagger}_{\vec{z}}\ket{\boldsymbol\Theta}\right)
|3ep⟩\displaystyle\ket{3_\text{ep}} :=∂∂t0,za​|ΨdCC-1-S1⟩=Ξ^​(∑l→ψl→,a​al→†​|0⟩el⊗bz→†​|𝚯⟩).\displaystyle:=\frac{\partial}{\partial t^{a}_{0,z}}\ket{\Psi_{\text{dCC-1-S1}}}=\hat{\Xi}\left(\sum_{\vec{l}}\psi_{\vec{l},a}a^{\dagger}_{\vec{l}}\ket{0}_{\text{el}}\otimes b^{\dagger}_{\vec{z}}\ket{\boldsymbol\Theta}\right).

We see from the above that these states describe single electronic excitations and one phonon corrections to the ground state at first order. At the second order of excited state theory, the additional second-derivative states

|4pp⟩\displaystyle\ket{4_{\text{pp}}} :=∂2∂tz​∂tx​|ΨdCC-1-S1⟩=Ξ^​(∑l→ζl→​al→†​|0⟩el⊗bx†​bz†​|𝚯⟩+∑l→​k→γl→,k→​al→†​|0⟩el⊗bx†​bz†​bk→†​|𝚯⟩)\displaystyle:=\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial t_{z}\partial t_{x}}\ket{\Psi_{\text{dCC-1-S1}}}=\hat{\Xi}\left(\sum_{\vec{l}}\zeta_{\vec{l}}a^{\dagger}_{\vec{l}}\ket{0}_{\text{el}}\otimes b^{\dagger}_{x}b^{\dagger}_{z}\ket{\boldsymbol\Theta}+\sum_{\vec{l}\vec{k}}\gamma_{\vec{l},\vec{k}}a^{\dagger}_{\vec{l}}\ket{0}_{\text{el}}\otimes b^{\dagger}_{x}b^{\dagger}_{z}b^{\dagger}_{\vec{k}}\ket{\boldsymbol\Theta}\right) (A41)
|5ep⟩\displaystyle\ket{5_{\text{ep}}} :=∂2∂t0,za​∂tx​|ΨdCC-1-S1⟩=Ξ^​(∑l→ψl→,a​al→†​|0⟩el⊗bz→†​bx→†​|𝚯⟩)\displaystyle:=\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial t^{a}_{0,z}\partial t_{x}}\ket{\Psi_{\text{dCC-1-S1}}}=\hat{\Xi}\left(\sum_{\vec{l}}\psi_{\vec{l},a}a^{\dagger}_{\vec{l}}\ket{0}_{\text{el}}\otimes b^{\dagger}_{\vec{z}}b^{\dagger}_{\vec{x}}\ket{\boldsymbol\Theta}\right)

which incorporate two-phonon corrections on top of the ground state. We note that mixed-partial derivatives of electron and phonon degrees of freedom yield states identical to the tangent directions corresponding to first derivatives of the coupled electron–phonon parameters, and second-order electronic derivatives vanish, so that these directions do not contribute to the second-order manifold. All subsequent required matrix elements involving these states may be computed in an analogous way to the first-order ground-state theory.

The projected Hamiltonian and overlap matrices are organized in blocks corresponding to the electronic, phononic, coupled electron–phonon, two-phonon, and coupled electron-two-phonon (e, p, ep, pp, epp) sectors, as illustrated in Fig. A3. In the present work, we evaluate and store these matrices explicitly and solve the resulting generalized eigenvalue problem directly, which is sufficient for the benchmark systems considered here. For larger-dimensional problems, the same formalism can be paired with iterative eigensolvers [28] and sparse solvers [78] by using matrix-vector products without storing the full matrix, with the associated costs summarized in Table 2.

Appendix G Finite-temperature matrix elements

In this appendix we sketch the evaluation of necessary matrix elements needed in the first-order finite-temperature implementation. To begin, the explicit time- and temperature-dependence from the finite-temperature trace and Heisenberg time evolution may be absorbed into the coherent-state basis as

|𝝈⁡(β,t)⟩\displaystyle\ket{\boldsymbol\sigma(\beta,t)} :=e∑m​n(−β−i​t)​ωm​n​bm†​bn​|𝜶⟩\displaystyle:=e^{\sum_{mn}(-\beta-it)\omega_{mn}b^{\dagger}_{m}b_{n}}\ket{\boldsymbol\alpha} (A42)
=exp⁡([e−(β+i​t)​𝝎⋅𝜶]T​𝐛†)​|0⟩\displaystyle=\exp(\left[e^{-(\beta+ it)\boldsymbol\omega} \cdot\boldsymbol{\alpha}\right]^T \mathbf{b}^\dagger)\ket{0}

using a BCH expansion, where 𝝎\bm{\omega} is the matrix describing the phonon dispersion, 𝜶\bm{\alpha} the vector of coherent state shifts per site, and 𝐛†\mathbf{b}^{\dagger} a vector containing creation operators per site (b1†,⋯,bN†)(b^{\dagger}_{1},\cdots,b^{\dagger}_{N}). As seen in the preceding equation, the time- and temperature-dependence are accounted for by introducing a time and temperature dependence into the coherent state shifts of the tracing coherent state basis.

When evaluating the finite-temperature Green’s function, we encounter integrals of matrix elements of the form

\displaystyle ∫d​𝜶​d​𝜶¯(2​π​i)Ne−∑zα¯zαz⟨𝝈⁡(β,t)|𝚯−d⟩⟨𝚯−d′|𝜶⟩\displaystyle\int\frac{d\bm{\alpha}d\bar{\bm{\alpha}}}{(2\pi i)^{N}}e^{-\sum_{z}\bar{\alpha}_{z}\alpha_{z}}\bra{\boldsymbol\sigma(\beta, t)}\ket{\boldsymbol\Theta_{-d}}\bra{\boldsymbol\Theta_{-d'}}\ket{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} (A43)
=\displaystyle= ∫d​𝜶​d​𝜶¯(2​π​i)N​exp(−∑zα¯zαz+∑zΘ∗z−d′αz+∑z[e−(β+i​t)​𝝎⋅𝜶]∗zΘz−d).\displaystyle\int\frac{d\bm{\alpha}d\bar{\bm{\alpha}}}{(2\pi i)^{N}}\exp(-\sum_z \bar{\alpha}_z\alpha_z + \sum_z \Theta^*_{z-d'}\alpha_z + \sum_z \left[e^{-(\beta+ it)\boldsymbol\omega} \cdot\boldsymbol\alpha\right]^*_z \Theta_{z-d}).

Similarly to the second-order energy evaluation, this may be written in matrix-vector notation as

∫d​𝜶​d​𝜶¯(2​π​i)N​exp⁡(−α†​α+ud′†​α+α†​vd)\int\frac{d\bm{\alpha}d\bar{\bm{\alpha}}}{(2\pi i)^{N}}\exp(- \alpha^\dagger\alpha+ u^\dagger_{d'} \alpha+ \alpha^\dagger v_d) (A44)

where α=(α1,⋯,αN)\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\cdots,\alpha_{N}), M=e−(β+i​t)​𝝎M=e^{-(\beta+it)\bm{\omega}}, ud=(Θ1−d,⋯,ΘN−d)u_{d}=(\Theta_{1-d},\cdots,\Theta_{N-d}), and vd=M†​udv_{d}=M^{\dagger}u_{d}. Shifting the variables of integration, this can then be simplified to

I⁡(ud′†,vd):=eud′†​vd​∫d​𝜶′​d​𝜶¯′(2​π​i)N​e−α′⁣†​α′=eud′†​vdI(u^{\dagger}_{d^{\prime}},v_{d}):=e^{u^{\dagger}_{d^{\prime}}v_{d}}\int\frac{d\bm{\alpha}^{\prime}d\bar{\bm{\alpha}}^{\prime}}{(2\pi i)^{N}}e^{-\alpha^{\prime\dagger}\alpha^{\prime}}=e^{u^{\dagger}_{d^{\prime}}v_{d}} (A45)

using the fact that the latter half of the expression is equivalent to identity. As done previously, the generating function I⁡(ud′†,vd)I(u^{\dagger}_{d^{\prime}},v_{d}) may then be used to compute matrix elements involving strings of bosonic operators inserted between the coherent state factors in Eq. A43. Insertion of bzb_{z} between the rightmost coherent state factors introduces a linear factor of αz\alpha_{z} into the coherent state integral, and can be interpreted as a derivative of the generating function with respect to ud′†u^{\dagger}_{d^{\prime}}

∫d​𝜶​d​𝜶¯(2​π​i)N⋯⟨𝚯−d′|bz|𝜶⟩→ezT⋅∂∂ud′†I(ud′†,vd)=ezT⋅vdeud′†​vd.\int\frac{d\bm{\alpha}d\bar{\bm{\alpha}}}{(2\pi i)^{N}}\cdots\bra{\boldsymbol\Theta_{-d'}}b_{z}\ket{\boldsymbol\alpha}\rightarrow e^{T}_{z}\cdot\frac{\partial}{\partial u^{\dagger}_{d^{\prime}}}I(u^{\dagger}_{{d^{\prime}}},v_{d})=e^{T}_{z}\cdot v_{d}e^{u^{\dagger}_{d^{\prime}}v_{d}}. (A46)

Similarly, insertion of bz†b^{\dagger}_{z} between the leftmost coherent state factors in Eq. A43 introduces a linear factor of [α†​M†]z[\alpha^{\dagger}M^{\dagger}]_{z} which may be interpreted as a derivative with respect to vdv_{d} as

∫d​𝜶​d​𝜶¯(2​π​i)Ne−∑zα¯zαz⟨𝝈⁡(β,t)|bz†|𝚯−d⟩⋯→ezT⋅(M†)T∂∂vdI(ud′†,vd)=ezT⋅(M∗ud′∗)eud′†​vd.\int\frac{d\bm{\alpha}d\bar{\bm{\alpha}}}{(2\pi i)^{N}}e^{-\sum_{z}\bar{\alpha}_{z}\alpha_{z}}\bra{\boldsymbol\sigma(\beta, t)}b^{\dagger}_{z}\ket{\boldsymbol\Theta_{-d}}\cdots\rightarrow e^{T}_{z}\cdot(M^{\dagger})^{T}\frac{\partial}{\partial v_{d}}I(u^{\dagger}_{d^{\prime}},v_{d})=e^{T}_{z}\cdot(M^{*}u^{*}_{d^{\prime}})e^{u^{\dagger}_{d^{\prime}}v_{d}}. (A47)

Matrix elements involving a greater number of bosonic operator insertions may be computed by evaluating the corresponding chained higher-derivatives detailed above.

Appendix H Analysis of the optical conductivity

H.1 Perturbative analysis

In this appendix, we develop an intuition for the qualitative differences which arise in the observed 2D Holstein and BSSH optical conductivities. As the coupling we use (g=1g=1) is comparatively weak in the two-dimensional case, we utilize one-phonon perturbation theory on top of the non-interacting electron–phonon problem with ground state at zero-momentum |g(0)⟩=c0†​|vac⟩\ket{g^{(0)}}=c^{\dagger}_{0}\ket{\text{vac}}. For simplicity, we will assume a single electronic band, as in the Holstein and BSSH models.

Defining the unperturbed one-phonon states with zero total momentum,

|μ𝐪(0)⟩:=c𝐪†​bμ−𝐪†​|vac⟩,\ket{\mu_\mathbf{q}^{(0)}}:=c^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{q}}b^{\dagger}_{\mu_{-\mathbf{q}}}\ket{\text{vac}}, (A48)

we have that these states have, for the unperturbed Hamiltonian

H^0=∑𝐤ϵ𝐤​c𝐤†​c𝐤+∑μ𝐪ωμ𝐪​bμ𝐪†​bμ𝐪,\hat{H}_{0}=\sum_{\mathbf{k}}\epsilon_{\mathbf{k}}c^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{k}}c_{\mathbf{k}}+\sum_{\mu_{\mathbf{q}}}\omega_{\mu_{\mathbf{q}}}b^{\dagger}_{\mu_{\mathbf{q}}}b_{\mu_{\mathbf{q}}}, (A49)

an unperturbed energy of Eμ𝐪(0)=ϵ𝐪+ωμ−𝐪E^{(0)}_{\mu_{\mathbf{q}}}=\epsilon_{\mathbf{q}}+\omega_{\mu_{-\mathbf{q}}}. For the 2D Holstein and BSSH models, inserting the tight-binding dispersion and single optical phonon frequency ω0\omega_{0} allows us to simplify this to

Eμ𝐪(0)=ω0−2​t​(cos⁡qx+cos⁡qy).E^{(0)}_{\mu_{\mathbf{q}}}=\omega_{0}-2t(\cos q_{x}+\cos q_{y}). (A50)

Using the bare-electronic energy of E0(0)=−4​tE^{(0)}_{0}=-4t, we may then define the energy difference

Δ𝐪\displaystyle\Delta_{\mathbf{q}} =Eμ𝐪(0)−E0(0)\displaystyle=E^{(0)}_{\mu_{\mathbf{q}}}-E^{(0)}_{0} (A51)
=ω0+2​t​(2−cos⁡qx−cos⁡qy).\displaystyle=\omega_{0}+2t(2-\cos q_{x}-\cos q_{y}).

This equation has the simple interpretation as the excitation energy required to create a phonon and move the electron from the band minimum to a finite momentum. From this, we see that the one-phonon continuum energetically extends from ω0\omega_{0} at 𝐪=(0,0)\mathbf{q}=(0,0) to ω0+8​t\omega_{0}+8t at the zone edge 𝐪=(π,π)\mathbf{q}=(\pi,\pi).

For a generic electron–phonon interaction term V^\hat{V}, we then have from first-order perturbation theory [116] the interacting eigenstates to first-order in the coupling, defining Vμ𝐪=⟨μ𝐪(0)|V^|g(0)⟩V_{\mu_{\mathbf{q}}}=\langle{\mu_{\mathbf{q}}^{(0)}}|\hat{V}|{g^{(0)}}\rangle,

|g(1)⟩=|g(0)⟩−∑μ𝐪Vμ𝐪Δ𝐪​|μ𝐪(0)⟩|g^{(1)}\rangle=|{g^{(0)}}\rangle-\sum_{\mu_{\mathbf{q}}}\frac{V_{\mu_{\mathbf{q}}}}{\Delta_{\mathbf{q}}}|\mu_{\mathbf{q}}^{(0)}\rangle (A52)

and

|μ𝐪(1)⟩=|μ𝐪(0)⟩+Vμ𝐪∗Δ𝐪​|g(0)⟩.|\mu_{\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}\rangle=|\mu_{\mathbf{q}}^{(0)}\rangle+\frac{V^{*}_{\mu_{\mathbf{q}}}}{\Delta_{\mathbf{q}}}|{g^{(0)}}\rangle. (A53)

We further decompose the relevant current operator j^x\hat{j}_{x} exactly into a component independent of and linear in the coupling,

j^x=j^x(0)+j^x(1),\hat{j}_{x}=\hat{j}^{(0)}_{x}+\hat{j}_{x}^{(1)}, (A54)

after which the matrix elements in the regular part of the optical conductivity Eq. 25 can be written

ℳμ𝐪\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{\mu_{\mathbf{q}}} =⟨μ𝐪(1)|j^x|g(1)⟩\displaystyle=\langle\mu_{\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}|\hat{j}_{x}|g^{(1)}\rangle (A55)
≈−∑μ𝐪′Vμ𝐪′Δ𝐪⟨μ(0)𝐪|j^(0)x|μ′(0)𝐪⟩+Vμ𝐪∗Δ𝐪⟨g(0)|j^(0)x|g(0)⟩+⟨μ𝐪(0)|j^(1)x|g(0)⟩\displaystyle\approx-\sum_{\mu_{\mathbf{q}}^{\prime}}\frac{V_{\mu_{\mathbf{q}}^{\prime}}}{\Delta_{\mathbf{q}}}\langle{\mu^{(0)}_{\mathbf{q}}}|\hat{j}^{(0)}_{x}|{\mu^{\prime}}^{(0)}_{\mathbf{q}}\rangle+\frac{V^{*}_{\mu_{\mathbf{q}}}}{\Delta_{\mathbf{q}}}\langle g^{(0)}|\hat{j}^{(0)}_{x}|g^{(0)}\rangle+\langle\mu_{\mathbf{q}}^{(0)}|\hat{j}^{(1)}_{x}|g^{(0)}\rangle

to first order. For the 2D nearest-neighbor tight-binding dispersions we consider, j^x(0)\hat{j}_{x}^{(0)} takes the momentum space form

j^x(0)=2​t​∑𝐤sin⁡kx​c𝐤†​c𝐤.\hat{j}_{x}^{(0)}=2t\sum_{\mathbf{k}}\sin k_{x}c^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{k}}c_{\mathbf{k}}. (A56)

The BSSH model additionally has a phonon-mediated current term of the form

j^x(1)=−2​gN∑𝐤𝐪ei​qx/2sin⁡(kx+qx2)c𝐤+𝐪†c𝐤(bx−𝐪†+bx𝐪)\hat{j}^{(1)}_{x}=-\frac{2g}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}\mathbf{q}}e^{iq_{x}/2}\sin(k_x + \frac{q_x}{2})c^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q}}c_{\mathbf{k}}(b^{\dagger}_{x_{\mathbf{-q}}}+b_{x_{\mathbf{q}}}) (A57)

for the xx-direction. Now, letting vx​(𝐤)=∂ϵ𝐤∂kx=2​t​sin⁡kxv_{x}(\mathbf{k})=\frac{\partial\epsilon_{\mathbf{k}}}{\partial k_{x}}=2t\sin k_{x}, we have that the general first-order matrix element (Eq. A55) can be written as

ℳμ𝐪=−Vμ𝐪Δ𝐪​vx​(q)+Vμ𝐪∗Δ𝐪​vx​(0)+Jμ𝐪(1),\mathcal{M}_{\mu_{\mathbf{q}}}=-\frac{V_{\mu_{\mathbf{q}}}}{\Delta_{\mathbf{q}}}v_{x}(q)+\frac{V^{*}_{\mu_{\mathbf{q}}}}{\Delta_{\mathbf{q}}}v_{x}(0)+J^{(1)}_{\mu_{\mathbf{q}}}, (A58)

where we have defined Jμ𝐪(1)=⟨μ𝐪(0)|j^x(1)|g(0)⟩J_{\mu_{\mathbf{q}}}^{(1)}=\langle\mu^{(0)}_{\mathbf{q}}|\hat{j}^{(1)}_{x}|g^{(0)}\rangle. A further simplification is obtained by noting that the electronic band minimum occurs at 𝐤=0\mathbf{k}=0, which results in the second term containing vx​(0)v_{x}(0) vanishing. We now substitute the current operators for Holstein and BSSH into these general expressions.

For the Holstein model, the first-order coupling element may be simply evaluated to be

V𝐪H=gN.V_{\mathbf{q}}^{\text{H}}=\frac{g}{\sqrt{N}}. (A59)

As the Holstein model supports a current derived exactly from the bare electronic operator, with no component coming from the coupling, the relevant optical conductivity matrix element then becomes

ℳ𝐪H=−2​g​tN​Δ𝐪​sin⁡(qx).\mathcal{M}^{\text{H}}_{\mathbf{q}}=-\frac{2gt}{\sqrt{N}\Delta_{\mathbf{q}}}\sin(q_x). (A60)

At the one-phonon level, the regular part of the optical conductivity then becomes

σregH​(ω)=πV​∑𝐪4​t2​g2N​Δq3​sin2⁡(qx)​δ​(ω−Δ𝐪).\sigma^{\text{H}}_{\text{reg}}(\omega)=\frac{\pi}{V}\sum_{\mathbf{q}}\frac{4t^{2}g^{2}}{N\Delta_{q}^{3}}\sin^{2}(q_{x})\delta(\omega-\Delta_{\mathbf{q}}). (A61)

On the other hand, the BSSH model has a current piece contributed by the electron–phonon coupling and thus has a non-zero Jμ𝐪(1)J^{(1)}_{\mu_{\mathbf{q}}}. Evaluating this expression yields

Jμ𝐪(1)\displaystyle J^{(1)}_{\mu_{\mathbf{q}}} =−2​gN∑𝐤′​𝐪′ei​qx/2sin⁡(kx′+qx′2)⟨μ(0)𝐪|c†𝐤′+𝐪′c𝐤(b†x−𝐪′+bx𝐪′)|g(0)⟩\displaystyle=-\frac{2g}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\mathbf{q}^{\prime}}e^{iq_{x}/2}\sin(k_x' + \frac{q_x'}{2})\langle\mu^{(0)}_{\mathbf{q}}|c^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}+\mathbf{q}^{\prime}}c_{\mathbf{k}}(b^{\dagger}_{x_{-\mathbf{q}^{\prime}}}+b_{x_{\mathbf{q}^{\prime}}})|g^{(0)}\rangle (A62)
=−2​gN​ei​qx/2​sin⁡(qx2)​δμ​x.\displaystyle=-\frac{2g}{\sqrt{N}}e^{iq_{x}/2}\sin(\frac{q_x}{2})\delta_{\mu x}.

Additionally, the first piece contributes as

Vμ𝐪BSSH\displaystyle V^{\text{BSSH}}_{\mu_{\mathbf{q}}} =gN​∑𝐤′​μ𝐪′′[e(i​kμ′′+qμ′′)+e−i​kμ′′]​⟨μ𝐪(0)|c𝐤′+𝐪′†​c𝐤′​(bμ−𝐪′′†+bμ𝐪′′)|g(0)⟩\displaystyle=\frac{g}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\mu^{\prime}_{\mathbf{q}^{\prime}}}[e^{(ik^{\prime}_{\mu^{\prime}}+q^{\prime}_{\mu^{\prime}})}+e^{-ik^{\prime}_{\mu^{\prime}}}]\langle{\mu^{(0)}_{\mathbf{q}}}|c^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}+\mathbf{q}^{\prime}}c_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}(b^{\dagger}_{\mu^{\prime}_{-\mathbf{q}^{\prime}}}+b_{\mu^{\prime}_{\mathbf{q}^{\prime}}})|g^{(0)}\rangle (A63)
=gN​(ei​qμ+1)\displaystyle=\frac{g}{\sqrt{N}}(e^{iq_{\mu}}+1)
=2​gN​ei​qμ/2​cos⁡(qμ2).\displaystyle=\frac{2g}{\sqrt{N}}e^{iq_{\mu}/2}\cos(\frac{q_\mu}{2}).

The relevant BSSH optical matrix element then becomes

ℳregBSSH=−4​g​tN​Δ𝐪​ei​qμ/2​cos⁡(qμ2)​sin⁡(qx)−2​gN​ei​qx/2​sin⁡(qx2)​δμ​x.\mathcal{M}^{\text{BSSH}}_{\text{reg}}=-\frac{4gt}{\sqrt{N}\Delta_{\mathbf{q}}}e^{iq_{\mu}/2}\cos(\frac{q_\mu}{2})\sin(q_x)-\frac{2g}{\sqrt{N}}e^{iq_{x}/2}\sin(\frac{q_x}{2})\delta_{\mu x}. (A64)

Squaring this matrix element then yields the BSSH optical conductivity

σregBSSH​(ω)=4​π​g2V​N​∑𝐪[sin2⁡(qx2)Δ𝐪​[1+4​t​cos2​(qx2)Δ𝐪]2+4​t2​sin2⁡(qx)​cos2⁡(qy2)Δ𝐪3]​δ​(ω−Δ𝐪),\sigma^{\text{BSSH}}_{\text{reg}}(\omega)=\frac{4\pi g^{2}}{VN}\sum_{\mathbf{q}}\bigg[\frac{\sin^{2}(\frac{q_{x}}{2})}{\Delta_{\mathbf{q}}}\Big[1+\frac{4t\cos^{2}(\frac{q_{x}}{2})}{\Delta_{\mathbf{q}}}\Big]^{2}+\frac{4t^{2}\sin^{2}(q_{x})\cos^{2}(\frac{q_{y}}{2})}{\Delta_{\mathbf{q}}^{3}}\bigg]\delta(\omega-\Delta_{\mathbf{q}}), (A65)

where the last term is an indirect Holstein-like contribution.

H.2 Sector decomposition

The analysis above describes absorption out of the ground state. At finite temperature, initial states of nonzero total crystal momentum additionally contribute, and we characterize their absorption profiles with our tangent space response framework in Fig. A4. The inset shows the distribution of sector energies relative to the band minimum. The large number of states near the band maximum (capped by hybridization with the one-phonon continuum) and the large absorption feature of such states in the ω≃2−3\omega\simeq 2-3 region underlie the interpretation of the dominant finite-temperature absorption feature in Section V.3.
